title: The case that illustrates how Trump’s retribution campaign is falling short | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Donald Trump has long sworn his second term in office would bring with it a campaign of retribution against his perceived political enemies.

But ultimately, those efforts have proven largely ineffective – and at times disastrous – for the administration and its Justice Department, despite an exceedingly loyal attorney general and an FBI director who long billed himself asa deep-state attack dog.

Few cases better exemplify the continued failure in prosecuting Trump’s perceived enemies than one brought against former FBI officials in October. In two weeks, a federal judge tossed the charges after an FBI agent testified the case was built at the behest of the president, with FBI leadership listing potential charges and demanding constant updates from agents.

In his written order released this week dismissing the case, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui ridiculed prosecutors for bringing a politically charged case with “rampant errors and misstatements stemming from the slapdash nature of this investigation and prosecution.”

“If a high-profile case like this is so poorly executed, what can the public expect in the run-of-the-mill case with far less resources and oversight,” Faruqui wrote.

In mid-October, two former FBI officials whose previous work focused on nefarious foreign influence were charged with making false statements to lawmakers in 2023, allegedly misleading members of Congress as to the extent of their knowledge of the FBI’s investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop years earlier.

The ultimate charges, however, did not stem from the origins of the investigation into the former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, or the unit they worked for, the agency’s Foreign Influence Task Force, which focused in part on foreign efforts to interfere with US elections.

According to the agent, Bryan Witt, FBI Director Kash Patel ordered the agency’s Kansas City field office to investigate Floris and others on obstruction or conspiracy charges. That order, he said, came after Trump complained about Floris and other “rogue bureaucrats” during a primetime speech in July, claiming they buried intelligence showing China sought to help Joe Biden win the 2020 election, in part by manufacturing illegal ballots.

The president demanded the FBI and others investigate.

The next day, Patel gave the directive to start the probe, listing potential charges, Witt said.

Witt testified others at the FBI thought the investigation was a “witch hunt” and that he was concerned about the political nature of the case. The agent admitted that the evidence did not support the charges Patel listed nor the case Trump claimed. Instead, the agent said, during their search, investigators found claims around Hunter Biden’s laptop made by Floris and Benavides in two separate 2023 interviews the agents believed to be false.

“The takeaway for FBI staff is to be afraid,” Faruqui wrote in his order this week dismissing the case. “They are one tweet away from being prosecuted by their own government.”

Faruqui added: “The harm from this weaponization is metastasizing from current staff to future recruits. What sane person would join the FBI, particularly in the national security branch, under these circumstances? Starving the FBI of talented agents and analysts is a grave risk to our national security.”

Patel has overseen the firing of scores of agents who were assigned to investigations into Trump and his political enemies, as well as those seen to be acting in a way not sufficiently loyal to the president and his movement, lawsuits by fired agents have alleged.

Despite the victory for the former agents in the case, “the stain this prosecution leaves on the good names of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides is incalculable,” Faruqui wrote, noting the inherent cost of such prosecutions. “No matter what they do, they will never be able to escape their names being associated with this slapdash, politicized attack on them.”

The now-dismissed charges from October focused on statements Floris and Benavides made about their knowledge of the FBI’s investigation into Hunter Biden and his laptop. Prosecutors believed Floris and Benavides lied when they denied knowledge of certain facts records show they had been aware of years earlier.

Faruqui, however, found that several statements had been true and that other statements, made during roundabout, confusing questioning, were not knowingly false.

The judge noted FBI agent Witt made several errors in his own testimony about the investigation before the court, which “demonstrate how easy it is to forget something important.”

“The Court chalks up (Witt’s) mistakes to confusion and bad memory, just as it does for Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides,” he added. “Just as (Witt) concluded about his own misstatements, any misstatement of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides was ‘not an intentionally false statement.’”

Faruqui also found the government had not shown what motive the pair would have in lying to Congress by denying knowledge of a case and investigation that were already in full swing. Instead, Faruqi wrote that it was the government whose motivation “is clear” in their efforts to “appease President Trump.”

“Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides did not have a reason to interfere with the already full-throttle Congressional investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop,” he wrote. “There was no benefit Ms. Floris or Mr. Benavides received by making the allegedly false statements.”

Instead of fleshing out the case more fully, “getting to the truth interfered with the rush to charge,” the judge wrote of investigators’ efforts in the case.

“And the motive for that is clear: to appease President Trump in his campaign of retribution against the FBI and to score cheap political points to impact the midterm elections,” the judge wrote.

In a show of support, dozens of agents fired under Trump’s second term attended the hearing in early November when Faruqui first announced his decision to dismiss the case. Former acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll, who fought administration officials early in 2025 when they demanded lists of names of agents to purge and was subsequently fired, was also in attendance.
